newsitem.title: USA: Fed must be ready to act against inflation -- Parry.
newsitem.headline: Fed must be ready to act against inflation -- Parry.

text.p: The Federal Reserve must be "ready to act" to head off increases in U.S. inflation before they begin to appear in price data, San Francisco Federal Reserve Bank President Robert Parry said.
"It will be especially important during this period to be keenly alert to any signs of increases in inflation pressures.
"Indeed, we must be ready to act to head off increases in inflation before they begin to show up in the inflation data," Parry said in Munich, Germany.
A copy of the Parry's speech was made available in New York.
The San Francisco Fed chief also said the U.S. economy is performing "very well, indeed surprisingly well."
Parry added that the current economic expansion, which will reach its seventh year later this month, is "not showing many signs of age."

Parry, who is a current voting member of the Fed's policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee, said the U.S. dollar's strength "probably subtracted a couple of tenths of a percent from our consumer price inflation in 1996.
"If the dollar remains at its present level, we expect about the same effect this year," Parry added.

The San Francisco Fed head also said the U.S. central bank is following closely Europe's progress towards monetary union, including fiscal austerity measures being pursued by Economic Community nations to satisfy the Maastricht criteria.
"Of special interest is how much this anticipated contraction in fiscal policy will slow Europe's growth and reduce demand for our exports," Parry said.
Parry reiterated his preference for a Fed mandate which included price stability as the central bank's main goal.

"As for me, I would prefer to have a clear mandate from Congress that our main goal in price stability," he said, adding, "I think it's safe to say that price stability does not mean zero inflation to most FOMC members."

The central banker also said the Fed has to look at a wide variety of economic indicators and data when formulating monetary policy. "In other words, we look at everything," the San Francisco Fed head said.
Parry said the wage-moderating effect that job insecurity has on U.S. inflation is likely to be temporary.

"It seems unlikely that job insecurity can last for a long time in the face of healthy job market. At some point, workers will realize that there are a lot of job opportunities out there, and they will push for better wages," he said.
He added that the U.S. will see a reversal in the current downward trend of labor costs "at some point."
